notes: Shared by scan_secrets.py and the grep fallback in bi-kit-check. Each rule: id, severity (fix_now|consider), regex (Python/ripgrep compatible), plain-language why and fix.

rules.why: Anyone who can open this file (or the app's code) can log in as you.
rules.fix: Delete it, change the password, and let the app use its Snowflake connection or a Snowflake secret instead.

rules.why: A token in code works like a password and often has broad access.
rules.fix: Revoke the token, then store it as a Snowflake secret or let the app's connection authenticate.

rules.why: A private key in a file lets anyone authenticate as that user.
rules.fix: Remove the file from the project, rotate the key pair, and keep keys outside the project folder.

rules.why: This looks like a cloud access key.
rules.fix: Revoke it in AWS and use a Snowflake storage or external access integration instead.

rules.why: The connection string includes a password.
rules.fix: Use a named connection or the app's built-in Snowflake connection.

rules.why: The app runs with an admin role, so every viewer effectively gets admin-level data access.
rules.fix: Use the shared-app role from your company standards.

rules.why: The app is tied to one person's login; it breaks when they leave and hides who really ran queries.
rules.fix: Use the app's own connection (owner's or caller's rights) instead of a named user.

rules.why: Browser login only works on your laptop; a shared app can't use it.
rules.fix: Deployed apps use their Snowflake connection; keep personal logins in your local connections file.

rules.why: .env files usually hold credentials and are easy to share by accident.
rules.fix: Keep it out of the project you hand off, or move values into Snowflake secrets.
